opener.heading: Week 18: Bugs & Blooms 🌷
about: Flowers and insects run one arrangement between them, and Azlyn works both ends of it for seven days. She mashes petals into perfume, bashes their color into cloth with a wooden spoon, feeds the butterflies off a saucer, and rolls twenty balls of mud with wildflower seed through them. She follows a bumblebee on foot, names two snails, and counts everything with legs that lives round your house.

April turns into May on Saturday and the garden starts paying back at last, so most of this week happens outside or comes in on a tray. Four things outlast the seven days: the seed balls by the door, the bug hotel against the fence, the notebook square she draws on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday, and the sealed jar on the sill. The notebook pays out on Thursday. The other three do not pay out inside the week at all, so tell her that on Monday and again on Thursday.
azlyn: Flowers and insects feed each other. She carries pollen on a cotton ball bee, then watches a bumblebee do the real thing on Monday morning.
Tally marks stand in for things. One line per creature, then six stacks of paper squares, and the tallest stack answers the question without counting.
A drawing holds still. The same square of grass goes in her notebook on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday, and the three pages do not match.
Handling something alive. Snails lift on a paintbrush and never by the shell, stones go back the same way up, bees get watched from an arm's length.
Color comes out of a petal. Warm water pulls it, a wooden spoon prints it onto cloth, and yellow gives up nothing at all.
you: Smell is wired directly to memory in a way the other senses aren't
Fairness is the strongest moral instinct a three-year-old has
A record makes slow change perceptible
Keep environmental talk local and hopeful at this age
Giving something a face changes how a child treats it
Tally marks are her first taste of representing data
A closed system is a big idea in a small jar
shopping: Flowers past their best, 2 bunches (the reduced shelf is the place)
Fresh petals and flat leaves off the garden
A sprig of mint or rosemary
A banana and an apple, left out from Thursday to go soft
A lettuce leaf, or a dandelion one off the grass strip
All-purpose flour, 1 cup, plus 2 tbsp of flour or cocoa for the pollen
A small plant or 3 cuttings (a supermarket mint pot works)
A packet of wildflower or herb seed
A clump of moss (pull it off a wall on Wednesday's way in)
One large clear jar with a lid, pasta sauce or pickle size
A saucer, or a plastic tub lid
A shallow dish, a small bowl and a large mixing bowl
Paper cupcake cases or paper cups, 6
A spoon, a teaspoon and a table knife
A small funnel, or paper to fold one
Soft paintbrushes, 2, one of them small
Thick paper or thin card, 8 sheets
Stiff card off a cereal box
Paper towels, and coffee filters if you have them
Washable markers (permanent ones do nothing on wet paper)
Clear parcel or packing tape, 1 roll (it has to be clear for Thursday)
Short sticks, a handful, and dry grass, straw or dead leaves
A brick or a heavy stone
An old white pillowcase or T-shirt
A damp cloth, a dish towel and a towel
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 10 months this week. He cruises the furniture, points at whatever he wants named, and understands no well enough to stop for a second before carrying on. He turns 11 months on Wednesday the 5th, lets go of the sofa to stand on his own. He babbles in long strings with the tune of a sentence in them, so answer the tune and leave him a gap.

days.title: Petals and Perfume
days.prepTonight: Stand any past-it flowers in a pitcher on the table, with three clean jam jars, the sieve and a wooden spoon beside them.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Bashing the Color Out of the Petals

opening.title: Taking a Flower to Pieces
opening.need: 3 flowers past their best · 1 white plate · 1 damp cloth.
steps: Hand her a whole flower and let her pull it apart onto the plate. Three piles: petals, leaves, and the middle with the pollen on it.
Name the parts while her hands are on them: petal, stem, leaf, pollen. Rub a fingertip through the pollen and look at the yellow on it. You smell it and tell her what it smells of.
Tell her the petal pile becomes perfume at 9:15. Wipe her hands with the damp cloth before they reach her face.

main.title: Perfume in a Jam Jar
materials: 1 bunch of past-it flowers, or petals off the garden
1 small funnel, or a cone folded from paper
steps: Petals into the first jar, hers from this morning and the rest off the bunch, until it is half full. Press them down with the spoon.
Tear the mint or rosemary and drop it in. Squeeze the half lemon over the top, pips and all.
Pour warm water from the pitcher over the petals until the jar is two thirds full. Warm, not hot.
Give her the wooden spoon and let her mash. It takes ten minutes. The water turns the color of the flowers.
Lid on, one good shake, then hold the sieve over the second jar and pour it through. Press the pulp with the spoon, tip it away and rinse the first jar.
Stand the funnel in the third jar and let her share the perfume between all three. Labels, pencil, and she says whose is whose. Three jars and four people, so somebody doubles up.
main.tip: Warm water pulls more smell out than cold, and the lot turns in two or three days, so use it today. Kreston's jar gets sniffed and never worn.

outside.title: Filling the Petal Bag
paras: Everything this afternoon needs comes off this walk, so hand her the paper bag at the door. Work low: the flowerbed by the wall where the tulips have blown open and dropped, the violets in the grass strip, a flat leaf off anything with a strong vein down the middle. Leave whatever is still standing on a stem in somebody's front yard. Ask her which colors will print, take her guess as it comes, and write it on the bag in pencil so you can read it back at one o'clock.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and points at whatever he wants named. Walk him along the flowerbed at your hip and answer every point, including the fourth one. Back at the table, give him his own wooden spoon on the high chair tray. He picks it up with finger and thumb, drops it over the side and wants it back, and it goes in his mouth where a petal must not.

second.title: Bashing the Color Out of the Petals
second.intro: The color in a petal comes out under a wooden spoon and prints straight onto cloth.
materials: 1 old white pillowcase or T-shirt, or 4 sheets of thick paper
1 wooden spoon or a rolling pin
steps: Lay the chopping board on the table and spread the pillowcase over it, one layer thick. Tape the corners down so it cannot shift.
She lays petals face down with gaps between them. Pull the stems and fat middles off first, since thick things smear.
Add two or three flat leaves. A leaf prints its veins.
Cover the lot with a sheet of baking paper and tape two corners of that down as well.
Hand her the wooden spoon and let her tap. Steady taps over every petal until the color comes through the baking paper.
Peel the paper back and lift the flattened petals off with paper towels. Look at what stayed behind.
Slide the cloth along, tape it on a clean patch and start again. Leave it flat over a chair back to dry.
second.tip: Dark petals print hardest and yellow tends to give nothing at all. Let her waste four or five finding that out for herself.

alternatives: Petals in a tray of water with a spoon, and nothing else.
Glue the flattened petals onto card instead of printing them.
Sort this morning's petals by color into an egg box.
Draw round the leaves and color inside the outlines.
outAgain: Playgroup, with the printed pillowcase in the bag to show
A friend's garden, where the flowers are different from yours
The park, for the blossom lying under the big trees
A walk to post a jar of perfume through somebody's door
The corner store for lemons, since she used yours

aroundWorld.title: The Insects People Send For 🐝
paras: Some insects arrive by delivery. Growers in France and California order ladybugs by the boxful to eat the aphids off a crop. Dutch tomato growers buy bumblebee colonies, because a greenhouse has no wind in it and the flowers need shaking. Every spring American beekeepers truck their hives to the almond orchards of California, which is the largest movement of bees on earth.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Honey on toast, and tell her which insect made it. Kreston gets none of it, because honey is off limits under one year old.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: One honeybee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life.

days.krestonPM: Kreston is 10 months and cruising, so he arrives at the table edge the moment the spoon starts banging. Give him his own end of it: a sheet of baking paper taped flat to his tray. He flattens it with both palms while she hammers.

insight.headline: Smell is wired directly to memory in a way the other senses aren't.
paras: Everything Azlyn sees and hears goes through a relay station in the middle of her brain before it reaches memory and feeling. Smell skips the relay. The nerves in her nose run to the olfactory bulb, which sits next door to the hippocampus and the amygdala, so a smell arrives with a memory and a feeling attached. That is why one can knock the wind out of you thirty years on. The smells she meets at three are the ones she will recognize at forty, and a jar of mashed petals files itself somewhere permanent. Name what she is smelling while her nose is still in it, because the word files itself alongside.

days.safety: Daffodil sap, foxglove and lily are toxic if chewed, and she has garden flowers in her hands all day. Nothing goes near a mouth, hers or Kreston's, and both get their hands washed before snack. Kreston is 10 months and cruises to whatever sits at his height, so the glass jars stay at the back of the table. The perfume gets a label, and it is not a drink.

days.title: A Share for the Bugs
days.prepTonight: Leave a banana and an apple out of the fridge to go soft overnight, and put the sugar, a saucer and a shallow dish on the counter.

opening.title: Cutting the Fair Shares
opening.need: 1 soft banana and 1 soft apple · 1 table knife · 2 plates.
steps: Ask her how many people live in the house. Four. Then ask who else in the yard eats fruit.
Give her the table knife and the banana and let her cut the shares. You do the apple. The pieces will be uneven and the count off. Leave both.
One plate for the people, one for the bugs. The family plate goes back for snack, the bug plate goes out at 9:15.

main.title: The Butterfly Plate
materials: 1 saucer or a plastic tub lid
steps: Tip the bug share onto the saucer and let her squash it flat with her thumb.
Tip the sugar into the shallow dish, add a splash of warm water and let her stir with a finger until the grains vanish.
Soak the sponge in it, squeeze it once, and set it on the saucer next to the fruit.
Rinse the dish, fill it a thumb deep and stand the pebbles in it. Bees drown in open water and need a stone to land on.
Pick the spot together: full sun, up on a wall, clear of the door, the stroller and anywhere you eat. Saucer down, dish beside it, chalk a ring round it.
Check it at 11:00, after lunch and before dinner. Flies and ants come first, so tell her that now.
main.tip: Butterflies want it rotten, so a banana gone black beats a fresh one. The plate does its best work tomorrow.

outside.title: The Ant Trail
paras: Ants are out in force by the first of May. Find a line along a paving joint and follow it until it goes underground. Put a crumb from her snack half an inch off the trail and sit back. The first ant to find it comes back with company.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and got a share this morning because Azlyn counted him in. Put his banana on his tray while she carries the bug plate out. Outside, sit him facing the ant line. He tracks small moving things and points at them to show you.

second.title: A Butterfly for Every Person
second.intro: Color bleeding through wet paper towels takes four seconds and she cannot predict any of it.
materials: Paper towels or coffee filters, 6 sheets
1 small bowl of water and 1 teaspoon
Tape and 1 length of string to hang them
steps: Lay a sheet of paper towels flat on the tray. Fat blobs and thick stripes of marker, no pictures, white gaps between.
Dip the teaspoon in the bowl and dribble water over the color. The lines spread and run together.
Lift the sheet with two hands, because it tears when wet, and lay it somewhere warm. Color the next while that one dries.
Gather a dry sheet along its middle into a concertina and clip a clothespin over the pinch. Wings both sides, clothespin as the body.
Twist a pipe cleaner round the top of the clothespin for antennae, or tie on a short length of string.
One butterfly per person. She hands them out and says who gets which.
Lay the string along the table and let her clip the butterflies onto it, then tape it up across the window frame above the catch.
second.tip: Washable markers bleed and permanent ones sit there doing nothing. Test one on a corner first.

alternatives: A folded coffee filter dipped corner-first in the water.
Clothespins and paper, no water, and color the wings in dry.
Cut butterfly shapes from yesterday's printed cloth.
Count what flies past the window in ten minutes.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of the month, and the bug case first
The garden center greenhouse, warm and full of things flying
A bus into town, if the museum line has beaten you
The park with the big flowerbeds, and count what is on them
Straight home to the window butterflies, if the morning was enough
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 10 months and the museum is ceiling from where he sits. Take him out in the biggest, quietest room and let him cruise a bench with your hand at his back. He points at whatever is high up and lit, so follow the point and name it. Forty minutes, then the stroller.

insight.headline: Fairness is the strongest moral instinct a three-year-old has.
paras: Azlyn will hand a cookie to a child she has never met and refuse Kreston a crayon inside the same minute, and both come off the same instinct. Three year olds track who got what with an accuracy that outstrips their counting. Put four grapes and two children in front of her and she splits them two and two long before she can tell you what two and two makes. Sharing with a butterfly she has never seen stretches the same muscle, and it costs her something real, which is the part that works. Let her set the size of the bug share.

days.safety: Sugar water and rotting fruit pull in wasps as well as butterflies. Site the plate well away from the door, the stroller and anywhere you eat, and neither child stands over it. Nobody swats anything. If a wasp comes to her, stand still with her and let it leave. Tape the butterfly string above the window catch, out of reach from the sill, and take it down at bedtime, because string at his height is a strangulation risk. Count the clothespins onto the line and count them off again.

days.title: The Same Square of Grass
days.prepTonight: Find a sheet of letter paper, four craft sticks or garden sticks, a ball of string and four clothespins, and stand them by the back door.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Four Sticks and a Piece of String

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Flower That Opens on the Water

opening.title: One Sheet, Eight Pages
opening.need: 1 sheet of letter paper · 1 pair of adult scissors · 1 pencil.
steps: Fold the sheet in half three times, letting her press each crease with her thumb, letting her press each crease with her thumb. Open it flat and count the eight boxes.
Fold it back in half the long way and cut along the center crease to the middle. You cut, she holds. Push the ends together and it opens into a book.
She writes her name on the front in pencil. Everything this week goes in here.

main.title: Four Sticks and a Piece of String
materials: 1 jam jar of water, used as a magnifier
steps: Let her choose the square: somewhere she can kneel, that nobody is mowing, and that she can see from the door.
Push the four sticks into the ground in a square, an arm's length a side. Tape round the top of each so they show from the house.
Run the string round all four and hold it with a clothespin at each stick.
Both of you down on your fronts. Count out loud what is in there: flowers, different leaves, anything moving. Stand the jam jar of water in front of something small and look through the glass.
Page one of the notebook. She draws what is inside with the crayons, you write the date and her words underneath in pencil.
Nothing else goes on page one. She draws the same square on Tuesday and Thursday, on pages two and three.
main.tip: Do not move the string when the first page comes out thin. Three dandelions and a pill bug is the measurement.

outside.title: Sidewalk Crack Flowers
paras: Walk the street with your eyes down. Dandelions, chickweed, moss and the odd violet come up through cracks in the sidewalk and out of the joint where the wall meets the path. Ask her how a flower gets into a crack with no soil in it. Count how many you pass before the corner, and pick none of them.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and understands no, which he shows by stopping for a second and then carrying on. The square of grass is the one thing he cannot crawl through today, so put him down the far side of you with a stick of his own, sanded blunt and longer than his forearm. He turns it over and works the grain with his thumb.

second.title: The Flower That Opens on the Water
second.intro: Paper takes on water and swells along its fibers, enough to push a folded petal open with nobody touching it.
steps: Draw a flower on a sheet with a crayon: a middle and six fat petals. Cut it out with the adult scissors while she holds the sheet.
She colors it, both sides. The more crayon goes on, the longer the paper takes to soak.
Fold each petal in to the middle, one lapping over the next, until it makes a bud in her palm.
Fill the bowl with two inches of water and stand it in the middle of the table.
Lay the bud on the surface, folds up, and take her hands away. Count out loud. It opens on its own inside thirty seconds.
Do the rest, changing one thing each time: more crayon, tighter folds, a bigger flower. Ask her which will be slowest.
Tip the water out the moment she is finished and dry the table with the towel.
second.tip: The last one can sit on the water while she watches it go to mush, and then it comes out with the water. Nothing stays on the table.

alternatives: Fold and float paper boats in the same bowl instead.
Draw the square of grass again from memory, indoors.
Tear paper petals and stick them on a card flower.
Cups and a sieve in the sink, no plan at all.
outAgain: The sunset walk, and it stays light past eight this month, so take the long loop
Feeding the ducks with the last of the soft bread
A new playground two streets past your usual one
The long way round, past the square she clipped out this morning
A scooter run to the mailbox and back
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 10 months and stands at the sofa arm for whole minutes. Once the bowl is emptied, hand him the wet towel. He drags it and drapes it over his head, a game he found this month.

insight.headline: A record makes slow change perceptible.
paras: Azlyn cannot see a plant grow. The change runs slower than a three year old's memory can hold, and last week for her is a fog with a few bright things in it. A drawing fixes one day in a form she can hold up against another one. Thursday's page beside Sunday's page does the work her memory cannot: two dandelions become five, the bare patch fills in, something has legs that was not there before. She is using a notebook the way a scientist uses one, for the same reason. Keep the wrong drawings, because the comparison needs both ends.

days.safety: A bowl of water at floor height and a 10 month old who pulls up on furniture. Two inches is enough to drown in. The bowl goes on the table or stays within your arm's reach, and it gets tipped out the moment she is finished. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Food for the Bees
days.prepTonight: Fill a bucket with garden soil or open the compost bag and stand it by the door, with the sieve, a bowl and newspaper.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Seed Balls for the Bare Patch

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Watering the Pot by the Door

opening.title: Sieving the Soil
opening.need: 2 cups garden soil or compost · 1 sieve · 1 large bowl · newspaper.
steps: Spread the newspaper over the table and stand the bowl in the middle of it.
Hand her the sieve and let her shake soil through by the handful. Stones and roots stay on top.
Look at what stayed in the sieve before you tip it back outside. Hands away from her face until they are washed.

main.title: Seed Balls for the Bare Patch
materials: 1 packet wildflower or herb seed (substitute: seed shaken out of a dandelion head, or seeds scooped from a supermarket tomato)
steps: Newspaper still down, sieved soil in the bowl. Sieve another scoop if there is less than two cups in there.
Add the cup of flour on top and let her mix the two dry with both hands until the color is even.
Water from the pitcher, a splash at a time. Stop when a squeezed handful holds its shape. Too wet, and a handful more soil brings it back.
Tip the seed in and fold it through with her hands so it runs all the way through.
Roll balls the size of a walnut between her palms and line them up on the baking tray. Aim for twenty.
Carry five out to the bare corner by the door and press them in with her thumb while they are soft. The rest dry on the tray, somewhere warm and out of reach.
main.tip: Do not bury them. A seed ball sits on the surface and waits for rain.

outside.title: Following One Bumblebee
paras: Bumblebees are heavy, loud and slow enough to follow on foot. The first week of May is the best of the year for it, because the dandelions are at their peak and the queens are out working them. Pick one working the dandelions and walk with it. Count the flowers it lands on before it goes over a fence, and watch the yellow build up on its back legs. Stay an arm's length back the whole time.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and will put soil in his mouth given four seconds alone with it. Sit him the far side of the newspaper with his own bowl of dry flour. He points at everything Azlyn does, so name it back: rolling, pressing, filling.

second.title: Carrying the Pollen
second.intro: Pollen moves because it sticks to a fuzzy body. The whole business runs on one cotton ball and two spoons of flour.
materials: 6 paper cupcake cases or paper cups
2 tbsp all-purpose flour, or cocoa, as the pollen
1 cotton ball taped to a clothespin, as the bee
steps: Open the six cupcake cases out and let her color the insides with the crayons, one color each.
Tape each case down onto the tray, spread apart, so they stay put when she lands on them.
Tape the cotton ball to the clothespin. She holds the clothespin, and the cotton ball is the fuzzy back of the bee.
Brush a pinch of flour into two of the six cases with the small paintbrush. The other four stay clean, and she checks that.
Fly the bee into a floury flower and press it down. Look at the cotton ball, then fly to a clean flower and press again.
Keep going, flower to flower. After twenty trips, count how many of the six have flour in them.
Pull the cases off the tray, stand them a meter apart round the room, and let her run it again.
second.tip: Cocoa shows up better than flour and it smells of something. Either way the sleeve of her top gets pollinated.

alternatives: Cotton ball bee on a string, flown by hand, no flowers.
Paint flowers on paper and stop there.
Sort the leftover seed by size on a dark plate.
Blow flour off a spoon outside and follow it.
outAgain: The neighborhood park, and find the tree the bees are on
The grass strip at the end of the road, thick with dandelions
A walk past the front yard she likes the look of
The green with a ball, if she has had enough of looking
The community garden, to see what other people are putting in
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 10 months and cruising, and grass is harder work than carpet. Stand him at the park bench and let him work along it, then set him down on the grass. He will hate the feel of it and then pull it up in fistfuls. Watch his hands, because grass goes in the mouth like everything else.

insight.headline: Keep environmental talk local and hopeful at this age.
paras: Azlyn cannot picture a rainforest or a decade. She can picture the bare corner by your door, and she can picture bees on it. Children who meet the big environmental story before they have any power over it end up holding the worry with none of the agency, and three is early for that. Give her the version she can act on: this patch had nothing on it, we put seeds there, look at it in July. Caring for one square meter she can reach builds the same instinct, and it leaves her feeling useful. The wide version of the story keeps until she is old enough to do something with it.

days.safety: Hands washed after soil and before food, both children. Compost and garden soil carry bacteria and neither of them should be mouthing it. Bees get watched and never touched or trapped, and nobody swings at one.

days.title: The Snails Get Names
days.prepTonight: Save six to eight cardboard tubes, cut four strips off a corrugated box, and put the shoebox and the packing tape on the table.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Bug Hotel by the Fence

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Two Snails and a Wet Tray

opening.title: Rolling the Little Rooms
opening.need: 3 strips of corrugated card · 3 cardboard tubes · packing tape.
steps: Roll one strip into a spiral so the ridges make tunnels, then let her roll the other two. Hers come out loose, which is better.
Push a spiral into each tube. If one springs out, wrap tape round the roll first and try again.
Hold a tube up to her eye and let her look down it. The gaps are the rooms.

main.title: The Bug Hotel by the Fence
materials: Dry grass, straw or dead leaves
steps: Take the lid off the shoebox and stand the box on its long side so the opening faces you. The lid goes underneath.
Cut the tubes down with the scissors so they finish flush with the front. You cut, she holds each one against the box.
Pack the tubes in on their sides until nothing rattles. Roll the fourth strip of card into a spiral and wedge it in a corner.
Push short sticks in on end to fill the gaps, then press dry grass into what is left. Nothing should fall out when she tips it.
Run packing tape round the box twice, or tie string round it both ways, so it holds once it has been rained on.
Wedge it against the fence, opening away from the weather and off the wet ground if you can. Brick on top.
main.tip: Nothing moves in today and she will look anyway. Tell her first: pill bugs within days, spiders after that, bees by the end of summer.

outside.title: Turning Over the Stones
paras: Every flat stone, log and upturned pot has a colony under it. Lift, look, and put it back the same way up, because it is somebody's roof. Pill bugs, worms, centipedes, and on a damp May morning, snails. Take two or three snails and a leaf indoors in a tub for this afternoon, and chalk a cross on the stone each one came off.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months, and short sticks, small stones and snails are all mouth-sized for him. Keep the build up on the table and give him a spare tube, too long to fit in his mouth, down on the floor. He bangs it, finds it makes a different noise on carpet, and does it fourteen more times.

second.title: Two Snails and a Wet Tray
second.intro: Two snails from the morning hunt get an afternoon as guests.
materials: 1 baking tray or a large plastic lid
2–3 snails or pill bugs from the morning hunt
steps: Wet the tray all over with the cloth. A dry surface is no good to a snail.
Lift each snail on with the soft paintbrush, under the foot and never by the shell. Never pull a snail off a surface it has gripped.
She names them. Write the names on the paper and let her draw each shell in crayon, spiral and all.
Set the leaf at one end and sit back while they find it. It takes longer than she expects.
Outside, chalk a start and a finish line on a paving slab, a hand's width apart, and wipe the slab damp.
Lift two snails to the start with the brush, put the leaf past the finish, hands off. The winner wins nothing.
Back on the wet tray, then back to their own chalked stones before dinner. Wash hands, and leave the notebook and the crayons out, because she draws page two of the clipped square at 4:15.
second.tip: A snail pulled into its shell wants leaving alone, and comes out in a few minutes on wet ground.

alternatives: Pill bugs instead, which are faster and easier to hold.
Draw a snail's spiral on paper, round and round, ten times.
Build a snail run out of the leftover tubes.
Wet a paving slab and see what comes out from under the pot.
outAgain: Swimming, and the pool is quiet on a Tuesday
The park on the way home, if the pool session is short
Indoor playground, if the pool is shut for maintenance
A splash in the yard with the tray and the hose instead
The library, a day early, for a snail book
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 10 months and holds the rail in the shallow end while his legs work. Give him the edge to cruise with your hands either side. He understands no now, though never lean on it: your hands stay on him. Twenty minutes and out before he goes cold.

insight.headline: Giving something a face changes how a child treats it.
paras: The minute a snail has a name, Azlyn stops carrying it by the shell and starts talking to it. Naming does something you can watch happen: she gives it wants, a home to get back to and a preference between two leaves, then handles it as though all of that is true. Treating an animal as a person is a step toward taking someone else's view rather than a mistake to correct. She practices on a snail because a snail is safe to be wrong about. The same machinery goes to work on Kreston. Use her names out loud all day, and take her word for what the snail wants.

days.safety: Snails and slugs carry parasites and soil bacteria. Hands scrubbed after handling and before any food, and nothing goes near a face. Snails, small stones and short sticks are all mouth-sized for Kreston at 10 months, so the tray stays up on the table indoors, and he goes in the stroller with the brake on for the slab race outside. The scissors stay with you. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Big Bug Count
days.prepTonight: Cut a piece of stiff card off a cereal box and leave it out with the ruler, two sharp pencils, the crayons and the masking tape.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Six Boxes and a Picture Each

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Same Count on the Green

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Turning the Marks into a Picture

opening.title: Six Boxes and a Picture Each
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 piece of stiff card · 1 ruler · 1 pencil · crayons · masking tape.
steps: Tape the sheet of paper along its top edge onto the stiff card. That is her clipboard.
Rule five lines down the page so it comes out in six columns. Her hand on the ruler, yours on the pencil.
She draws one creature at the top of each column in crayon: ant, pill bug, snail, bee, spider, worm.

main.title: The Big Bug Count
materials: 1 clear cup with a paper lid, as a bug pot
1 jam jar of water as a magnifier
steps: Sun hat on, clipboard under her arm, one pencil in her hand and the spare in your pocket, because the first gets dropped.
Show her the mark once. One line for one creature, in the column under its picture.
Start at the front step and work round the house in one direction. Under stones, up the wall, in the long grass.
For anything worth a longer look, put the clear cup over it and slide the paper lid underneath. Stand the jam jar of water beside it and look through both.
Anything that needs moving gets moved with the soft paintbrush. Fingers stay off, and whatever came out of a stone goes back under it.
Come in when the page is full or she is finished, and leave every mark as she made it.
main.tip: Count the same pill bug twice if she finds it twice. Arguing the point costs you the rest of the hour and gains her nothing.

outside.title: The Same Count on the Green
paras: Take the clipboard and the spare pencil to the green at the end of the road and run the count again on ground nobody looks after. Different grass, different bugs. The numbers are in the long stuff, so wade in with her rather than working from the path.

days.infant: Kreston turns 11 months today. He lets go of the furniture and stands on his own for a second or two before sitting down hard, and he runs that experiment all morning. Put him on grass for it. He answers your voice with his own noise on the walk, so leave a gap after everything you say to him.

second.title: Turning the Marks into a Picture
second.intro: Her tally sheet answers a question she cannot read off it yet. Stuck up in columns, the answer is the tallest one.
materials: 1 ruler or a strip of straight card
Sticky labels, or paper torn into squares
The tally sheet from this morning
steps: Big sheet on the table the long way round. Rule a line along the bottom with the ruler and mark six spaces, one per bug.
She draws the same six creatures along the bottom in crayon, copying her own pictures off the morning sheet.
Take the first column of tallies. Count the marks out loud and let her stick that many labels in a stack going up from her drawing.
Do the other five the same way. She sticks, you count and hand them over, and every square sits on top of the last.
Stand back and look at it from the door. The tallest stack is the winner.
Ask which one she thought would win before she started, and write her answer along the top.
Glue the morning's tally sheet into the bottom corner so both live on one page, and put it on the wall at her height.
second.tip: Keep the squares the same size and touching, or the tallest stack stops meaning the biggest number.

alternatives: Sort the six drawings into things that fly and things that do not.
Stack coins or buttons in columns instead of sticking paper.
Count what is on one flower for ten minutes and nothing else.
Draw the morning's biggest bug at life size.
outAgain: Indoor playground, the between-week one, and go for the quiet late session
The library, if you would rather have books than noise
The park, since it stays light and warm until dinner now
A friend's house, with the graph rolled up under her arm
The green again, to check the count in the afternoon heat
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 11 months and indoor playground is where standing on his own costs nothing when it fails. Put him in the toddler pen and let him haul up on the padded blocks. He lets go, stands, wobbles and drops, over and over. Keep him out of the big-kid runs.

insight.headline: Tally marks are her first taste of representing data.
paras: One line for one pill bug is an idea with a lot packed into it. The mark on the page is not the pill bug. It stands in for the pill bug, and it holds still while the pill bug walks off. Azlyn cannot count past a handful with any reliability and she does not need to, because the marks do the remembering for her. This afternoon takes it a step on: the tallest stack answers the question with no counting at all. Reading a chart at nine rests on this, and it starts with a pencil line she made in the grass.

days.safety: Long grass in May means ticks, so check both children's hairlines, necks and behind the knees when you come in. Nettles are up and sting on contact. Bees and wasps get looked at through the jar and never picked up.

days.title: A Garden in a Jar
days.prepTonight: Pull a clump of moss off a wall on your way in and leave it in a saucer of water by the sink, with the big jar.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Flowers Between Two Pieces of Tape

opening.title: Scrubbing the Pebbles
opening.need: a handful of pebbles or gravel · 1 bowl of warm water · 1 old toothbrush · 1 dish towel.
steps: Pebbles into the bowl and let her scrub them with the toothbrush. The water goes brown fast.
Line the clean ones up on the dish towel to dry, biggest to smallest if she wants an order.
Tell her what they are for: spare water sits in the bottom of the jar and not in the roots.

main.title: The Jar That Waters Itself
materials: 1 large clear jar with a lid (a pasta sauce or pickle jar)
A handful of pebbles or gravel
1 clump of moss (off the wall last night)
1 small plant or 3 cuttings (a supermarket mint pot works)
steps: Tip the scrubbed pebbles into the jar, two fingers deep, and let her shake it flat.
Spoon in two cups of soil and press it down with the back of the spoon.
Dig a hole with the spoon and stand the plant or the cuttings in it. She firms the soil round the stems with her thumbs.
Press the moss down over the bare soil like a carpet, green side up, out to the glass.
Two spoonfuls of water from the pitcher and no more. Damp, not wet. Wipe the inside of the glass with the cloth so she can see in.
Lid on tight. She writes the date on the label in marker and it goes on the front. Stand it at the back of a bright sill, out of direct sun.
main.tip: It fogs up by tomorrow. If water runs down the glass all day, take the lid off for an hour. If it never fogs, one more spoonful.

outside.title: The Moss Hunt
paras: Moss grows where nothing else gets a hold: north-facing walls, the shady side of the shed, the joint between two paving slabs. Take a spoon and a tub and collect three kinds. One will be flat, one will look like a forest half an inch high, and one comes up in cushions.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and pulls up on anything that holds still. Give him his own saucer of wet moss on the floor with you sitting right there. He will squeeze it and try to eat it, so this is a both-hands-on job or it does not happen.

second.title: Flowers Between Two Pieces of Tape
second.intro: Sealed between two strips of tape, a flower keeps its color and the light comes through it.
materials: The pressed flowers from Friday, or fresh flat petals put under a heavy book at breakfast
steps: Pull an arm's length of packing tape off the roll and lay it sticky side up. Two short tabs off the roll hold the ends down.
She lays the pressed flowers along it face down and spaced out. Anything with a lump in it will not seal.
Lay a second strip of tape over the top, sticky side down, and press the air out from the middle with her thumb.
Peel the whole strip up off the table. Hold it against the window and look at what the light does.
Fold thin card in half, pencil a window on the front, and cut through both layers with the adult scissors.
Tape the strip inside the fold so it shows through, and let her write on the frame in pencil.

Tape a loop of string to the back and hang it against the glass. Leave the notebook by the back door for 4:15: she draws page three kneeling at the clipped square, then the three pages go side by side on the table with Sunday's on the left.
second.tip: Press the tape down hard along every edge. Air left in there goes cloudy in a week, and the ones she seals flat still look right at Christmas.

alternatives: Tape flowers straight onto the window with no frame at all.
Press more flowers under books for next week.
Draw round the frames and color the windows in.
Sort the pressed flowers by which kept their color.
outAgain: The hardware store, for a bag of gravel and a second jar
The garden center, to see what is flowering this week
The park, to check whether the bumblebee tree is still busy
A walk to deliver a taped flower frame to a neighbor
The corner store, and she carries the bag home
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 11 months and the hardware store is a wall of nameable things. Keep him in the cart seat or the carrier, because everything at his height is small, sharp or heavy. Say the word for what he points at and wait a beat.

insight.headline: A closed system is a big idea in a small jar.
paras: Water goes up through the soil into the plant, out through its leaves, onto the cold glass and back down as rain, and the lid means none of it leaves. Azlyn finds the fog inside the jar tomorrow morning and it lands as magic. Let it. The version she can hold at three is that the water goes round and comes back, which is the water cycle in one sentence and the reason the sea does not run out. She has a rainstorm on the windowsill she can check before breakfast for a year. Look at it with her when she asks, and let her tell you what changed overnight.

days.safety: A big glass jar full of wet soil is heavy, and Kreston is 11 months and standing. It lives at the back of a high sill, never on a low table or a sill he can pull up to. Hands washed after the soil, both children. The scissors stay with you.
